dataset.what_one_row_represents: In uk_prime_ministers.csv, one row is one person who has held the office of UK Prime Minister (real humans only), with their Wikidata ID, term start date, Oxford/Cambridge attendance flags, a classification, and the institutions they studied at.
dataset.time_range: 1721 (Robert Walpole) to 2024 (Keir Starmer); one row has no recorded term start
dataset.geographic_scope: United Kingdom (and pre-1801 Great Britain) prime ministers; universities Oxford and Cambridge

ana_01.label: The clean split: Oxford 2x PMs, Cambridge 2.6x Nobels
ana_01.content: The two universities divide elite British output almost perfectly down the middle. Oxford has produced 31 UK Prime Ministers to Cambridge's 15 — a 2.07x advantage in politics. Cambridge has 79 Nobel laureates linked by Wikidata's 'educated at' field to Oxford's 30 — a 2.63x advantage in science. The same two institutions, measured the same way, split the nation's elite into rulers and discoverers: Oxford is the Prime Minister factory, Cambridge the Nobel factory.

calculation.output:
Oxford 31 PMs vs Cambridge 15 -> 2.07x
Cambridge 79 Nobel vs Oxford 30 -> 2.63x

data_table.description: Oxford vs Cambridge across the two elite output categories

ana_02.label: Where all 59 PMs went to university
ana_02.content: Of the 59 people who have held the office of UK Prime Minister, the educational breakdown is: 30 attended Oxford only, 14 Cambridge only, 1 attended both (Henry Pelham), 10 went to another university, and 4 have no university recorded. Counting the dual-attender on both sides gives the headline totals of 31 Oxford and 15 Cambridge. Oxbridge together accounts for 45 of the 59 PMs — more than three quarters.

calculation.output: Oxford only 30; Cambridge only 14; Both 1; Oxford total 31; Cambridge total 15; Other 10; Unknown 4; TOTAL 59

data_table.description: Classification of all 59 UK PMs by university route

ana_03.label: Oxbridge produced 45 of 59 PMs (76%)
ana_03.content: Three quarters of all UK Prime Ministers passed through Oxford or Cambridge: 45 of 59, or 76.3%. Just 10 (16.9%) attended a different university and 4 (6.8%) have no university recorded at all. The concentration of national leadership in two institutions is the structural fact underneath the Oxford-vs-Cambridge contest.

calculation.output: Oxford 30 (50.8%); Cambridge 14 (23.7%); Both 1 (1.7%); Other 10 (16.9%); Unknown 4 (6.8%); Oxbridge total = 45/59 = 76.3%

data_table.description: Oxbridge vs non-Oxbridge share of all 59 PMs

ana_04.label: Cambridge's century-long PM drought
ana_04.content: Cambridge has not sent a Prime Minister to office since Stanley Baldwin, whose last premiership began in 1923 — over a century ago. Meanwhile every single Oxford-educated PM since the Second World War took office in the modern era: 13 of Oxford's PMs entered Downing Street from 1950 onward. Since 1937, every PM who attended an English university went to Oxford — Attlee, Eden, Macmillan, Douglas-Home, Wilson, Heath, Thatcher, Blair, Cameron, May, Johnson, Truss, Sunak and Starmer — the only modern exceptions being PMs who went elsewhere (Gordon Brown, Edinburgh) or to no university (Churchill, Callaghan, Major).

calculation.output:
Last Cambridge-attending PM to take office: Stanley Baldwin (1923)
Oxford PMs taking office in/after 1937: 14
Since 1937 the Oxford-educated PMs run from Attlee (1945) to Starmer (2024)

data_table.description: PMs taking office since 1937 and their university route (in office order)

ana_05.label: The regime change: Cambridge faded, Oxford surged
ana_05.content: Splitting PMs by era reveals a clean handover. In the 1700s the two universities were near-even (6 Oxford, 5 Cambridge, plus 1 who attended both). Cambridge stayed competitive through the 19th century but collapsed in the 20th: it produced 3 PMs in 1900-1949 and zero from 1950 onward. Oxford did the opposite — from 2 PMs in 1900-1949 it exploded to 13 in the 1950-present era, dwarfing every other route. The mirror image of Oxford's rise is Cambridge's political disappearance.

calculation.output:
1700s: Ox 6 Cam 5 Both 1 Other 1 Unk 1
1800-1849: Ox 5 Cam 4 Other 2
1850-1899: Ox 4 Cam 2 Other 1
1900-1949: Ox 2 Cam 3 Other 4 Unk 1
1950-present: Ox 13 Cam 0 Other 2 Unk 1

data_table.description: Count of PMs by era and university route

ana_06.label: Christ Church, Oxford: the single most prolific college
ana_06.content: One Oxford college towers over the rest as a PM factory: Christ Church has educated 13 of the 59 Prime Ministers — more than the entire University of Cambridge's 15, and roughly a fifth of all British PMs from a single college. They span from George Grenville (1763) through Gladstone and Salisbury to Anthony Eden and Alec Douglas-Home in the 20th century. No other single college comes close in the unambiguous count.

calculation.output:
PMs who attended Christ Church (Oxford): 13
George Grenville, Shelburne, Portland, Grenville, Liverpool, Canning, Peel, Derby, Gladstone, Salisbury, Rosebery, Eden, Douglas-Home

data_table.description: Christ Church-educated PMs vs whole-university totals, for scale

ana_07.label: The Eton-to-Oxford pipeline
ana_07.content: The elite route is even narrower than 'Oxford'. 20 of the 59 PMs attended Eton College, and 14 of them went on to Oxford — a single school-and-university funnel that produced almost a quarter of all British Prime Ministers, from George Grenville to David Cameron and Boris Johnson. The Eton-Oxford pairing, not Oxbridge in general, is the densest channel to Downing Street.

calculation.output:
PMs who attended Eton: 20
PMs who attended both Eton AND Oxford: 14

data_table.description: The narrowing elite funnel toward the premiership

ana_08.label: The PMs who skipped university entirely
ana_08.content: The Oxford pipeline is dominant but not absolute. Four PMs have no university recorded, two of them genuinely never attended: David Lloyd George (PM 1916), who trained as a solicitor, and James Callaghan (PM 1976), the only 20th-century PM never to attend university, who left school at sixteen. A further 10 PMs attended a non-Oxbridge institution — Edinburgh (John Russell, Gordon Brown), Glasgow (Bonar Law), Birmingham (Neville Chamberlain), or no higher institution at all (Winston Churchill, John Major). These exceptions show the elite channel can be bypassed, even at the very top.

calculation.output:
Unknown/no university recorded: 4 (incl. David Lloyd George, James Callaghan)
Other (non-Oxbridge) university: 10 (incl. Russell & Brown at Edinburgh, Bonar Law at Glasgow, Churchill, Major)

data_table.description: Non-Oxbridge PMs and where they were educated (or not)

ana_09.label: Total notable-alumni coverage (NOT enrolment)
ana_09.content: Wikidata records 39,259 notable alumni for Oxford and 31,284 for Cambridge — Oxford's coverage is 25.5% larger. But this is a coverage-biased count of people notable enough to have a Wikidata item with an 'educated at' field, NOT an enrolment figure, and it must never be read as 'Oxford is bigger'. When the elite outputs are scaled against this notability base, the specialisation sharpens rather than fades: Cambridge yields 25.25 Nobel laureates per 10,000 notable alumni versus Oxford's 7.64, while Oxford yields 7.90 PMs per 10,000 versus Cambridge's 4.79. The division of labour survives normalisation.

calculation.output:
Oxford 39259 vs Cambridge 31284 (Oxford +25.5%)
Oxford PMs/10k: 7.90, Cambridge PMs/10k: 4.79
Cambridge Nobel/10k: 25.25, Oxford Nobel/10k: 7.64

data_table.description: Elite output per 10,000 notable Wikidata alumni (relative, coverage-caveated)

caveats.content: 'Total alumni on Wikidata' (39,259 / 31,284) is coverage-biased — it counts only people notable enough to have a Wikidata item with an 'educated at' field, not enrolment. Never present as a headcount or as 'Oxford is bigger'.

Nobel counts use 'educated at', so a laureate may be linked as a former student OR a later academic affiliate. Describe as 'associated with' / 'linked to', not 'graduated from'. University PR uses broader 'affiliated' definitions and reports higher numbers (Cambridge ~120+, Oxford ~76).

The 59-PM total includes a couple of pre-1801 Great Britain prime ministers and one row (Basil Feilding) with no term_start date, so totals can differ by 1-2 from lists starting at a different date. Fictional PMs (Doctor Who, House of Cards) were filtered out.

College attribution counts raw college-name tokens; 'Trinity College' is ambiguous between Oxford and Cambridge, so college-level analysis leads with Christ Church (unambiguously Oxford) rather than Trinity.
